title: TB6-14323
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): They are appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying their claims for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (the "principal Appellant") and her minor children, XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX, and XXXX XXXX XXXX (the "minor Appellants"), are citizens of Nigeria. They are appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying their claims for refugee protection. The Appellants are requesting that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) set aside the RPD's negative determination and find that they are Convention refugees or persons in need of protection. In the alternative, the Appellants request the RAD refer the matter back to the RPD for redetermination by a differently constituted panel. The Appellants have not requested to submit new evidence and have not requested an oral hearing.

The principal Appellant was appointed to be the designated representative (DR) for the minor Appellants at the RPD proceeding, and she continues to be the DR for the minor Appellants for the purposes of this appeal.1 DETERMINATION OF THE APPEAL

Pursuant to section 111(1)(c) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD accepts the appeal and refers the matter back to the RPD for redetermination by a differently constituted panel.2 The RAD is unable to confirm or set aside the RPD's decision without hearing evidence presented to the RPD with respect to the credibility of the Appellants and whether there is a viable internal flight alternative (IFA) available to them. Background

The Appellants allege that they, and the principal Appellant's husband, have experienced a series of robberies, threats and attacks since 2009. In XXXX 2016, while the Appellants were in Canada, misfortune continued to befall her family, as well as the principal Appellant's husband's family. As a result, the principal Appellant's husband's family consulted an oracle about the family's string of bad luck, and the oracle stated that the misfortune was due to the principal Appellant being a witch. In order to end the family's problems, the oracle demanded that the principal Appellant undergo cleansing rituals, and that the minor Appellants undergo female circumcision and traditional rites. The Appellants fear the husband's family, the police, and unknown robbers.

The Appellants obtained a visa on August 12, 2015. The principal Appellant visited Canada alone in XXXX 2015 to destress and have a change in environment. The principal Appellant returned to Nigeria in XXXX 2015. On XXXX XXXX, 2016, the Appellants and the principal Appellant's husband arrived in Canada for a holiday. Shortly thereafter, the principal Appellant's husband returned to Nigeria because his business was robbed. Following this, the principal Appellant's husband's family consulted with the oracle. It was at this time that the oracle announced she was a witch and that the Appellants had to undergo cleansing rituals. The Appellants made an inland refugee claim on June 16, 2016. However, the principal Appellant's husband chose not to make a refugee claim.3

The Appellants had a refugee determination hearing on August 16, 2016. In a written decision issued on September 29, 2016, the RPD rejected the claims. The RPD panel found the principal Appellant's evidence in crucial areas to lack credibility and that her and husband were not trustworthy witnesses in the proceeding. Therefore, the RPD concluded that the Appellants do not have a well-founded fear of persecution on a Convention ground, or that they would not personally be subjected to a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or a danger of torture upon return to Nigeria.
The Appellants argue that the RPD erred in its assessment of their credibility and documentary evidence.

The recent Federal Court of Appeal decision, in Huruglica,4 provides the RAD with guidance in relation to the appropriate standard that the RAD must apply in reviewing decisions of a first-level administrative tribunal. The Federal Court of Appeal states: [103] I conclude from my statutory analysis that with respect to findings of fact (and mixed fact and law) such as the one involved here, which raised no issue of credibility of oral evidence, the RAD is to review RPD decisions applying the correctness standard. Thus, after carefully considering the RPD decision, the RAD carries out its own analysis of the record to determine whether, as submitted by the appellant, the RPD erred. Having done this, the RAD is to provide a final determination, either by confirming the RPD decision or setting it aside and substituting its own determination of the merits of the refugee claim. It is only when the RAD is of the opinion that it cannot provide such a final determination without hearing the oral evidence presented to the RPD that the matter can be referred back to the RPD for redetermination. No other interpretation of the relevant statutory provisions is reasonable.5

There are, however, cases where the RPD may enjoy a meaningful advantage over the RAD in making findings of fact or mixed fact and law, because such findings require an assessment of the credibility or weight to be given to oral evidence heard by the RPD.6 Although the RAD should sometimes exercise a degree of restraint before substituting its own determination in such cases, the issue of whether the circumstances warrant restraint, should be addressed on a case-by-case basis. The amount of deference given to the RPD's findings on credibility of oral evidence will depend on the advantage the RAD finds that the RPD has in a particular case.7 Having done this, the RAD will provide a final determination, by either confirming the RPD's decision or setting it aside and substituting its own determination. If it cannot do so without hearing oral evidence that was already heard by the RPD, it will refer the matter back for redetermination.

The Appellants argue the following issues in their appeal: 1) The RPD erred in its assessment of the Appellants' credibility;8 and, 2) The RPD erred in its assessment of the documentary evidence.9 ANALYSIS Credibility/Subjective Fear The RPD's Findings

The RPD determined that the Appellants' evidence lacked credibility in crucial areas of their claim and that the principal Appellant and the witness (her husband) were not trustworthy witnesses, as their conduct was not consistent with that of persons having the fear, risk or experiences they allege.10 The RPD's conclusion is based on the following two findings.

First, the RPD noted that prior to XXXX 2016, the principal Appellant's mother in-law accused her of being a witch during private heated arguments. In addition, her husband's family suggested on a number of occasions that her daughters undergo female circumcision in accordance with the husband's family's traditional beliefs. The principal Appellant testified that she was concerned about these accusations and threats at the time she visited Canada in XXXX 2015, and that these rites and rituals were first proposed as early as 2008. The RPD asked if she had concerns about these issues, why she did not make a refugee claim in XXXX 2015, or at the port-of-entry (POE) when the Appellants came to Canada for a holiday on XXXX XXXX, 2016. The principal Appellant explained that it was not until the oracle declared her to be a witch, that it was "treated with the greatest of seriousness." The RPD rejected this explanation as "unreliable" given that prior to the oracle's pronouncement, the principal Appellant and her husband considered the accusations of being a witch by family members, elders and community members to be very serious, frightening and dangerous.11

Second, the RPD found the principal Appellant's explanations for when she first knew that she could make a refugee claim in Canada unreliable and implausible. This was because the principal Appellant testified that although she disclosed to her half-sister in XXXX 2015 her personal and family circumstances that formed the basis of their refugee claim, she did not ask her half-sister to provide her with any advice about making a refugee claim in Canada.12 The RPD also noted that the principal Appellant's "significant inconsistent and contradictory assertions and explanations with respect to when she first knew that she could claim refugee status in Canada but allegedly did not know how to make that refugee claim remained unresolved in the proceeding."13

With respect to the Appellants' documentary evidence, the RPD stated it accepted the findings of symptomology of the principal Appellant contained in the psychological report, but that the report does not establish that her symptoms and conditions were caused by or related to her refugee claim allegations.14 The RPD later noted in its conclusion, without a finding or attributing weight to the Appellants' documents that, the National Documentation Package (NDP) for Nigeria "confirms widespread official and other corruption and the availability of personal documents such as those proffered."15 The Appellants' Argument

The Appellants submit that the RPD's reasoning was not intelligible or sufficiently clear, and that the points cited by the RPD, which were to demonstrate the Appellants' lack of credibility, were not based on a reasoned analysis of the evidence. Rather, the points cited by the RPD as being indicative of the Appellants' lack of credibility, standing alone, or in unison, fail to demonstrate they have a lack of credibility.16

With respect to the RPD's finding that the Appellants failed to advance their claim at the POE, the principal Appellant argues that the RPD misapprehended her evidence and that it was not until the oracle was consulted that her fear was heightened.17 In addition, the Appellant submits that the RPD erred by impugning the principal Appellant's credibility because she stated that she did not get any legal advice or information about the refugee or immigration process in Canada until June 2016, even though she applied for a student visa in April 2016. The Appellants argue that the RPD misconstrued the evidence, because she thought she was answering a question about the refugee claim, and not her student visa (immigration) application.18 The Appellants further contend that the RPD used tangential points to impugn the Appellants' credibility and relied on peripheral information to rebut the presumption of truthfulness. The RPD made no real attempt to engage with the core elements of the claims.19

In regard to the Appellants' documentary evidence, the Appellants submit that the RPD failed to engage with the psychological report, other than saying it did not establish her symptoms were a result of her refugee claim allegations. Moreover, the RPD completely ignored the affidavits from the principal Appellant's mother, husband, and husband's employee. Instead the RPD dismissed the documents because of the prevalence of fraudulent documents in Nigeria.20 The RAD's Assessment

The RAD agrees with the Appellants' overarching argument that the RPD's findings cannot sustain its conclusion that the Appellants lack credibility and are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection. The RAD finds the RPD's reasons were largely difficult to follow. In addition, the RPD erred in its credibility analysis in the following ways. First, the RPD did not make clear in its reasons which parts of the claimant's story it believed and which it did not. The RPD said it drew negative inferences but did not make a clear finding on each of the allegations. Second, the RPD did not consider all of the evidence in context. It was selective and looked for small implausibilities to build its case. Third, the courts have held that the RPD must make credibility findings in "clear and unmistakable terms", and supported by adequate reasons. The RPD did not do so in this case. Also, aspects of a witness's testimony which are found to be not credible must be specifically identified and the reasons for rejecting the testimony and the explanations put forward by the claimant must be intelligibly explained. In this case, as argued by the Appellant, the claimant did seem to provide reasonable explanations, which also meant that the RPD erred in its findings on those points.

In particular, the RAD notes that the RPD does not make clear and explicit credibility findings in its "analysis". Rather, the RPD simply finds on two occasions that the principal Appellant's explanation for not claiming earlier was "unreliable", and that her explanation for not seeking the advice of her half-sister was both "unreliable" and "implausible." Although the RPD refers to inconsistencies and contradictions about when she learned she could make a refugee claim in Canada, it is not clear which inconsistencies and contradictions it is referring to, and the RPD does not make a specific credibility finding on the alleged inconsistencies and contradictions. In essence, the RPD's "analysis" is largely a summary of the principal Appellant's and the witness' testimony, with two credibility findings. Moreover, the RPD's two findings relate to the Appellants' subjective fear. While the RAD disagrees with the Appellants' submissions that these were peripheral findings, since delay in claiming is a relevant and important consideration, it is well-established that delay in making a claim is not determinative.21 The RAD finds the decision lacking in actual analysis and that its two findings related to their delay in claiming to be insufficient to substantiate the RPD's negative determination.

The RAD also agrees with the Appellants' argument that the RPD ignored their documentary evidence. The RPD mentioned the psychological report and addressed it in a very perfunctory manner. In addition, the RPD did not even mention the Appellants' affidavits, and as a result, the RAD doubts that the RPD actually considered them. The RPD's blanket statement that the RPD rejected the documents because the NDP confirms widespread corruption and the availability of personal documents in Nigeria is clearly insufficient and lacks any analysis. The Federal Court has clearly stated that rejecting such documents, because there is a prevalence of fraudulent documents in a country, is an error.22

Despite these errors, the RAD is not in a position to find that the Appellants have established their allegations based on the record before it. Having reviewed the whole record, including the audio recording, the RAD has remaining questions which relate to the Appellants' credibility on core aspects of their claims, as well as whether the Appellants have a viable IFA in Nigeria.23 These were not all put to the Appellants before the RPD, and the RAD is unable to do so in this proceeding, since IFA is a new issue. The RPD made no findings on IFA in its decision, and the issue was not canvassed at the RPD hearing.24 CONCLUSION

After conducting its own analysis of the entire record, the RAD finds that the RPD's findings are inadequate and insufficient to maintain the determination that the Appellants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection. The RPD's determination stems from only two credibility findings related to their delay in claiming, which is not determinative.

However, the RAD is unable to confirm or set aside the RPD's decision without hearing evidence presented to the RPD with respect to the credibility of the Appellants and whether there is a viable IFA available to them. Therefore, the RAD is not in a position to find the Appellants face a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground, or on a balance of probabilities, would be personally subjected to a danger of torture, or face a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, if returned to Nigeria.

In this case, credibility and IFA issues remain outstanding on evidence presented to the RPD, and this evidence was not tested by the RPD. Where the RAD is unable to confirm, or set aside and substitute its own decision without hearing evidence that was presented to the RPD, section 111(2)(c) of the IRPA allows the RAD to return the case to the RPD for re-determination. The RAD chooses to do so in this case. Disposition

Accordingly, pursuant to section 111(1)(c) of the IRPA, the RAD allows the appeal and refers the matter to the RPD for re-determination by a differently constituted panel, to consider issues of credibility and whether there is a viable IFA in Nigeria.
